# Week 13: Measurement invariance {.unnumbered}

::: {.week-meta}
Core reading
: @byrne2016, chapter 7, pp. 227–262 (about 2 hours)

Data
: [Student Life Survey](../course/dataset.qmd), clean file: compare first-year with later-year students

Apps
: Invariance ladder; χ² difference test

Task style
: Application: apply the technique to the Student Life Survey (or your own data) with a checklist

:::

## By the end of this week you can

- Run configural, metric and scalar invariance tests in Amos.
- Compare nested models with Δχ² and ΔCFI.
- Locate a non-invariant parameter and test partial invariance.

## Warm-up

Answer from memory at the start of the session. It takes two minutes and makes earlier ideas easier to recall later.

1. In R3, what made two regression models nested?
2. Why does adding a constraint increase a model's df?

<details class="answers">
<summary>Check your answers</summary>

1. One was the other with some paths fixed at zero.
2. It reduces the number of free parameters.

</details>

## This week in brief

Before comparing groups, you need to show that the measure works the same way in each group. Measurement invariance is tested in steps: configural (same structure), metric (equal loadings) and scalar (equal intercepts). Each step is a nested model, compared with Δχ² or ΔCFI: the same idea as the hierarchical regression in [R3](../regression/r3-inference.qmd).

## In the session

- Setting up a multigroup analysis in Amos, including Analyze > Multiple-Group Analysis.
- The invariance sequence and what each step allows you to compare.
- Partial invariance: finding and freeing the non-invariant parameter.

## After the session

Read the core reading. Read @putnick2016 (open access) if you have time; it is the clearest short guide.

## Your task this week

1. Reproduce Byrne's configural model and her test of equal factor loadings. Read the rest of her sequence without running it.
2. Test the invariance of your Student Life measurement model across `year`. **Predict** which level will hold, then fill in this table:

| Model | χ² | df | Δχ² | Δdf | p | CFI | ΔCFI | Decision |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| Configural | | | — | — | — | | — | |
| Metric (loadings equal) | | | | | | | | |
| Scalar (loadings and intercepts equal) | | | | | | | | |
| Partial scalar (one intercept freed) | | | | | | | | |

3. If scalar invariance fails, find the item responsible (compare item means by group, and the modification indices). Read its wording: why might it behave differently for later-year students? Free its intercept and retest.

## For your SEM log

Write your answers in your log first; then compare.

1. What can you compare across groups once metric invariance holds? Once scalar invariance holds?
2. Which item was non-invariant, and why might that be?
3. When would you use ΔCFI rather than Δχ²?

<details class="answers model">
<summary>Compare with model answers (after writing your own)</summary>

1. Metric: variances, covariances and structural paths. Scalar: latent means as well.
2. An item about a behaviour that changes with the stage of study (such as attending every timetabled session) can shift for reasons unrelated to engagement itself.
3. With large samples, where Δχ² detects trivial differences. ΔCFI (a change of about .01 or less) is less sensitive to N (Cheung & Rensvold, 2002).

</details>
